candidates.core_provocation: In a hospital where doctors can transfer memories between patients, a woman wakes after surgery with the memories of a beloved patient who has just died. She believes the memories prove she is the dead patient’s murderer—until the hospital announces that the dead patient is now walking around in her body.
candidates.why_interesting: The reversal turns a familiar memory-transfer miracle into a tense question of who is alive, who is guilty, and whether memories belong to the person who experienced them.

candidates.core_provocation: A hospital uses a machine that removes one traumatic memory to save patients from psychological illness. A surgeon discovers that the patient scheduled to have her memory erased is the only person who remembers a medical disaster the hospital itself has caused—and the surgeon may be the person whose memory must be removed instead.
candidates.why_interesting: The immediate choice between healing one person and preserving the truth creates suspense while making memory a weapon controlled by an institution.

candidates.core_provocation: In a hospital where patients can record memories for later playback, a coma patient’s family watches a recording in which she calmly predicts the exact moment she will wake up—and names the family member who must be killed before then. When she wakes, she claims the recording is not her memory but a message from the future.
candidates.why_interesting: The story combines a concrete countdown with an unsettling reversal: the supposedly reliable evidence of memory may be an instruction from something that has not happened yet.

parsed.reason_for_choice: The third premise offers the clearest short-story engine: a hospital, a recording, a predicted waking time, and a specific threat create immediate tension and forward momentum. Its reversal also makes readers question whether memory is evidence of the past—or a tool for controlling the future.
